{{Short description|Mathematics study in geometry}}
In mathematics, '''derived noncommutative algebraic geometry''',<ref>{{cite journal |arxiv=0710.1937|doi=10.1112/plms/pds034|title=Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch-type formula for DG algebras|year=2013|last1=Shklyarov|first1=D.|journal=Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society|volume=106|pages=1–32|s2cid=5541558}} The reference notes that the name "derived noncommutative algebraic geometry" may not be standard. Some authors (e.g., {{Cite journal|last=Orlov|first=Dmitri|date=October 2018|title=Derived noncommutative schemes, geometric realizations, and finite dimensional algebras|arxiv=1808.02287|journal=Russian Mathematical Surveys|volume=73|issue=5|pages=865–918|doi=10.1070/RM9844|bibcode=2018RuMaS..73..865O|s2cid=119173796|issn=0036-0279}}) describe this field as the study of '''derived noncommutative schemes'''.</ref> the derived version of [[noncommutative algebraic geometry]], is the geometric study of [[derived category|derived categories]] and related constructions of [[triangulated category|triangulated categories]] using categorical tools. Some basic examples include the bounded derived category of coherent sheaves on a [[smooth variety|smooth]] [[algebraic variety|variety]], <math>D^b(X)</math>, called its derived category, or the derived category of [[perfect complex]]es on an algebraic variety, denoted <math>D_{\operatorname{perf}}(X)</math>. For instance, the derived category of coherent sheaves <math>D^b(X)</math> on a smooth projective variety can be used as an invariant of the underlying variety for many cases (if <math>X</math> has an [[ample line bundle|ample]] (anti-)[[canonical sheaf]]). Unfortunately, studying derived categories as geometric objects of themselves does not have a standardized name.

==Derived category of projective line==
The derived category of <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> is one of the motivating examples for derived non-commutative schemes due to its easy categorical structure. Recall that the [[Euler sequence]] of <math>\mathbb{P}^1</math> is the [[short exact sequence]]

: <math>0 \to \mathcal{O}(-2) \to \mathcal{O}(-1)^{\oplus 2} \to \mathcal{O} \to 0</math>

if we consider the two terms on the right as a complex, then we get the distinguished triangle

: <math>\mathcal{O}(-1)^{\oplus 2} \overset{\phi}{\rightarrow} \mathcal{O} \to \operatorname{Cone}(\phi) \overset{+1}{\rightarrow}.</math>

Since <math>\operatorname{Cone}(\phi) \cong \mathcal{O}(-2)[+1]</math> we have constructed this sheaf <math>\mathcal{O}(-2)</math> using only categorical tools. We could repeat this again by tensoring the Euler sequence by the flat sheaf <math>\mathcal{O}(-1)</math>, and apply the cone construction again. If we take the duals of the sheaves, then we can construct all of the line bundles in <math>\operatorname{Coh}(\mathbb{P}^1)</math> using only its triangulated structure. It turns out the correct way of studying derived categories from its objects and triangulated structure is with exceptional collections.

==Semiorthogonal decompositions and exceptional collections==
{{main|semiorthogonal decomposition}}
The technical tools for encoding this construction are semiorthogonal decompositions and exceptional collections.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Liu|first=Yijia|title=Superschool on Derived Categories|pages=35, 37, 38, 41|chapter=Semi-orthogonal Decompositions of Derived Categories}}</ref> A '''semiorthogonal decomposition''' of a triangulated category <math>\mathcal{T}</math> is a collection of full triangulated subcategories <math>\mathcal{T}_1,\ldots, \mathcal{T}_n</math> such that the following two properties hold

(1) For objects <math>T_i \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T}_i)</math> we have <math>\operatorname{Hom}(T_i, T_j) = 0</math> for <math>i > j</math>

(2) The subcategories <math>\mathcal{T}_i</math> generate <math>\mathcal{T}</math>, meaning every object <math>T \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})</math> can be decomposed in to a sequence of <math>T_i \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})</math>,

:<math>0 = T_n \to T_{n-1} \to \cdots \to T_1 \to T_0 = T</math>

such that <math>\operatorname{Cone}(T_i \to T_{i-1}) \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T}_i)</math>. Notice this is analogous to a filtration of an object in an [[abelian category]] such that the cokernels live in a specific subcategory.

We can specialize this a little further by considering exceptional collections of objects, which generate their own subcategories. An object <math>E</math> in a triangulated category is called '''exceptional''' if the following property holds

:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(E,E[+\ell]) = \begin{cases}
k &\text{if } \ell = 0 \\
0 &\text{if } \ell \neq 0
\end{cases}</math>

where <math>k</math> is the underlying field of the [[vector space]] of morphisms. A collection of exceptional objects <math>E_1, \ldots, E_r</math> is an '''exceptional collection''' of length <math>r</math> if for any <math>i > j</math> and any <math>\ell</math>, we have

:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(E_i, E_j[+\ell]) = 0</math>

and is a '''strong exceptional collection''' if in addition, for any <math>\ell \neq 0</math> and ''any'' <math>i, j</math>, we have

:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(E_i, E_j[+\ell]) = 0</math>

We can then decompose our triangulated category into the semiorthogonal decomposition

:<math>\mathcal{T} = \langle \mathcal{T}', E_1, \ldots, E_r \rangle </math>

where <math>\mathcal{T}' = \langle E_1, \ldots, E_r \rangle^\perp</math>, the subcategory of objects in <math>E \in \operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal{T})</math> such that <math>\operatorname{Hom}(E, E_i[+\ell]) = 0</math>. If in addition <math>\mathcal{T}' = 0</math> then the strong exceptional collection is called '''full'''.

==Beilinson's theorem==
Beilinson provided the first example of a full strong exceptional collection. In the derived category <math>D^b(\mathbb{P}^n)</math> the line bundles <math>\mathcal{O}(-n), \mathcal{O}(-n+1), \ldots, \mathcal{O}(-1), \mathcal{O}</math> form a full strong exceptional collection.<ref name=":0" /> He proves the theorem in two parts. First showing these objects are an exceptional collection and second by showing the diagonal <math>\mathcal{O}_\Delta</math> of <math>\mathbb{P}^n \times \mathbb{P}^n</math> has a resolution whose compositions are tensors of the pullback of the exceptional objects.

'''Technical Lemma'''

An exceptional collection of sheaves <math>E_1, E_2, \ldots, E_r</math> on <math>X</math> is full if there exists a resolution

:<math>0 \to p_1^*E_1 \otimes p_2^*F_1 \to \cdots \to p_1^*E_n \otimes p_2^*F_n \to \mathcal{O}_\Delta \to 0</math>

in <math>D^b(X\times X)</math> where <math>F_i</math> are arbitrary coherent sheaves on <math>X</math>.

Another way to reformulate this lemma for <math>X = \mathbb{P}^n</math> is by looking at the Koszul complex associated to<blockquote><math>\bigoplus_{i=0}^n \mathcal{O}(-D_i) \xrightarrow{\phi} \mathcal{O}</math></blockquote>where <math>D_i</math> are hyperplane divisors of <math>\mathbb{P}^n</math>. This gives the exact complex<blockquote><math>0 \to \mathcal{O}\left(-\sum_{i=1}^n D_i \right) \to \cdots \to
\bigoplus_{i \neq j}\mathcal{O}(-D_i - D_j) \to
\bigoplus_{i=1}^n\mathcal{O}(-D_i) \to \mathcal{O} \to 0</math></blockquote>which gives a way to construct <math>\mathcal{O}(-n-1)</math> using the sheaves <math>\mathcal{O}(-n),\ldots,\mathcal{O}(-1),\mathcal{O}</math>, since they are the sheaves used in all terms in the above exact sequence, except for

:<math>\mathcal{O}\left(-\sum_{i=0}^n D_i \right) \cong \mathcal{O}(-n-1)</math>

which gives a derived equivalence of the rest of the terms of the above complex with <math>\mathcal{O}(-n-1)</math>. For <math>n=2</math> the Koszul complex above is the exact complex<blockquote><math>0 \to \mathcal{O}(-3) \to \mathcal{O}(-2)\oplus\mathcal{O}(-2) \to \mathcal{O}(-1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(-1) \to \mathcal{O} \to 0</math></blockquote>giving the quasi isomorphism of <math>\mathcal{O}(-3)</math> with the complex<blockquote><math>0 \to \mathcal{O}(-2)\oplus\mathcal{O}(-2) \to \mathcal{O}(-1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(-1) \to \mathcal{O} \to 0</math></blockquote>

==Orlov's reconstruction theorem==
If <math>X</math> is a smooth projective variety with ample (anti-)canonical sheaf and there is an [[Equivalence of categories|equivalence]] of derived categories <math>F: D^b(X) \to D^b(Y)</math>, then there is an isomorphism of the underlying varieties.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Dolgachev|first=Igor|url=http://www.math.lsa.umich.edu/~idolga/derived9.pdf|title=Derived categories|pages=105–112}}</ref>

=== Sketch of proof ===
The proof starts out by analyzing two induced Serre functors on <math>D^b(Y)</math> and finding an isomorphism between them. It particular, it shows there is an object <math>\omega_Y = F(\omega_X)</math> which acts like the dualizing sheaf on <math>Y</math>. The isomorphism between these two functors gives an isomorphism of the set of underlying points of the derived categories. Then, what needs to be check is an ismorphism <math>F(\omega_X^{\otimes k}) \cong \omega_Y^{\otimes k}</math>, for any <math>k \in \mathbb{N}</math>, giving an isomorphism of canonical rings

: <math>A(X) = \bigoplus_{k=0}^\infty H^0(X,\omega_X^{\otimes k}) \cong \bigoplus_{k=0}^\infty H^0(Y,\omega_Y^{\otimes k})</math>

If <math>\omega_Y</math> can be shown to be (anti-)ample, then the proj of these rings will give an isomorphism <math>X \to Y</math>. All of the details are contained in Dolgachev's notes.

=== Failure of reconstruction ===
This theorem fails in the case <math>X</math> is Calabi–Yau, since <math>\omega_X \cong \mathcal{O}_X</math>, or is the product of a variety which is [[Calabi–Yau manifold|Calabi–Yau]]. [[Abelian variety|Abelian varieties]] are a class of examples where a reconstruction theorem could ''never'' hold. If <math>X</math> is an abelian variety and <math>\hat{X}</math> is its dual, the [[Fourier–Mukai transform]] with kernel <math>\mathcal{P}</math>, the Poincaré bundle,<ref>The Poincaré bundle <math>\mathcal{P}</math> on <math>X\times \hat{X}</math> is a line bundle which is trivial on <math>\{0\}\times\hat{X}</math> and <math>X\times\{0\}</math> and has the property <math>\mathcal{P}|_{X\times\{x\}}</math> is the line bundle represented by the point <math>x \in \hat{X}</math>.</ref> gives an equivalence

:<math>FM_{\mathcal{P}}:D^b(X) \to D^b(\hat{X})</math>
of derived categories. Since an abelian variety is generally not isomorphic to its dual, there are derived equivalent derived categories without isomorphic underlying varieties.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Mukai|first=Shigeru|date=1981|title=Duality between D(X) and D(X^) with its application to Picard sheaves|url=https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.nmj/1118786312|journal=Nagoya Math. J.|volume=81|pages=153–175|via=Project Euclid|doi=10.1017/S002776300001922X|doi-access=free}}</ref> There is an alternative theory of '''tensor triangulated geometry''' where we consider not only a triangulated category, but also a [[monoidal category|monoidal]] structure, i.e. a tensor product. This geometry has a full reconstruction theorem using the spectrum of categories.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.math.ucla.edu/~balmer/Pubfile/TTG.pdf|title=Tensor triangulated geometry|last=Balmer|first=Paul|date=2010|journal=Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians}}</ref>

=== Equivalences on K3 surfaces ===
[[K3 surface]]s are another class of examples where reconstruction fails due to their Calabi–Yau property. There is a criterion for determining whether or not two K3 surfaces are derived equivalent: the derived category of the K3 surface <math>D^b(X)</math> is derived equivalent to another K3 <math>D^b(Y)</math> if and only if there is a Hodge isometry <math>H^2(X, \mathbb{Z}) \to H^2(Y, \mathbb{Z})</math>, that is, an isomorphism of [[Hodge structure]].<ref name=":1" /> Moreover, this theorem is reflected in the motivic world as well, where the Chow motives are isomorphic if and only if there is an isometry of Hodge structures.<ref>{{cite arXiv|eprint=1705.04063|title=Motives of isogenous K3 surfaces|last=Huybrechts|first=Daniel|author-link=Daniel Huybrechts|date=2018|class=math.AG}}</ref>

=== Autoequivalences ===
One nice application of the proof of this theorem is the identification of autoequivalences of the derived category of a smooth projective variety with ample (anti-)canonical sheaf. This is given by
:<math>\operatorname{Auteq}(D^b(X)) \cong (\operatorname{Pic}(X)\rtimes \operatorname{Aut}(X))\times\mathbb{Z}</math>
Where an autoequivalence <math>F</math> is given by an automorphism <math>f:X\to X</math>, then tensored by a line bundle <math>\mathcal{L} \in \operatorname{Pic}(X)</math> and finally composed with a shift. Note that <math>\operatorname{Aut}(X)</math> acts on <math>\operatorname{Pic}(X)</math> via the polarization map, <math>g \mapsto g^*(L)\otimes L^{-1}</math>.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www-fourier.ujf-grenoble.fr/~mbrion/autos.pdf|title=Notes on Automorphism Groups of Projective Varieties|last=Brion|first=Michel|page=8|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200213231444/https://www-fourier.ujf-grenoble.fr/~mbrion/autos.pdf|archive-date=13 February 2020}}</ref>

== Relation with motives ==
The bounded derived category <math>D^b(X)</math> was used extensively in SGA6 to construct an [[intersection theory]] with <math>K(X)</math> and <math>Gr_\gamma K(X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}</math>. Since these objects are intimately relative with the [[Chow ring]] of <math>X</math>, its [[Motive (algebraic geometry)|chow motive]], Orlov asked the following question: given a [[fully faithful functor]]

: <math>F:D^b(X) \to D^b(Y)</math>

is there an induced map on the chow motives

: <math>f:M(X) \to M(Y)</math>

such that <math>M(X)</math> is a summand of <math>M(Y)</math>?<ref>{{cite journal|arxiv=math/0512620|title=Derived categories of coherent sheaves and motives|last=Orlov|first=Dmitri|journal=Russian Mathematical Surveys|volume=60|issue=6|pages=1242–1244|date=2011|doi=10.1070/RM2005v060n06ABEH004292|s2cid=11484447}}</ref> In the case of K3 surfaces, a similar result has been confirmed since derived equivalent K3 surfaces have an isometry of Hodge structures, which gives an isomorphism of motives.

== Derived category of singularities ==
On a smooth variety there is an equivalence between the derived category <math>D^b(X)</math> and the thick<ref>Meaning it is closed under extensions. Given any two objects <math>\mathcal{E}', \mathcal{E}''</math> in the subcategory, any object <math>\mathcal{E}</math> fitting into an exact sequence <math>0 \to \mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{E}'' \to 0</math> is also in the subcategory. In the triangulated case, this translates to the same conditions, but instead of an exact sequence, it is a distinguished triangle <math>\mathcal{E}' \to \mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{E}'' \to \mathcal{E}[+1]</math></ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gwern.net/docs/math/1990-thomason.pdf|title=Higher Algebraic K-Theory of Schemes and of Derived Categories|last1=Thomason|first1=R.W.|last2=Trobaugh|first2=Thomas|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190130235347/https://www.gwern.net/docs/math/1990-thomason.pdf|archive-date=30 January 2019}}</ref> full triangulated <math>D_{\operatorname{perf}}(X)</math> of perfect complexes. For [[Separated scheme|separated]], [[Noetherian scheme|Noetherian]] schemes of finite [[Krull dimension]] (called the '''ELF''' condition)<ref>Which he uses because of its nice properties: in particular every bounded complex of coherent sheaves <math>C^\bullet</math> has a resolution from a bounded above complex <math>P^\bullet \xrightarrow{\simeq} C^\bullet</math> such that <math>P^\bullet</math> is a complex of locally free sheaves of finite type.</ref> this is not the case, and Orlov defines the derived category of singularities as their difference using a quotient of categories. For an ELF scheme <math>X</math> its derived category of singularities is defined as

: <math>D_{sg}(X) := D^b(X)/D_\text{perf}(X)</math><ref>{{Cite arXiv|title=Triangulated Categories of Singularities and D-Branes in Landau–Ginzburg Models|last=Orlov|first=Dmitri|eprint=math/0302304|year=2003 }}</ref>

for a suitable definition of [[Localization of a category|localization]] of triangulated categories.

=== Construction of localization ===
Although localization of categories is defined for a class of morphisms <math>\Sigma</math> in the category closed under composition, we can construct such a class from a triangulated subcategory. Given a full triangulated subcategory <math>\mathcal{N} \subset \mathcal{T}</math> the class of morphisms <math>\Sigma(\mathcal{N})</math>, <math>s</math> in <math>\mathcal{T}</math> where <math>s</math> fits into a distinguished triangle<blockquote><math>X \xrightarrow{s} Y \to N \to X[+1]</math></blockquote>with <math>X,Y \in \mathcal{T}</math> and <math>N \in \mathcal{N}</math>. It can be checked this forms a multiplicative system using the octahedral axiom for distinguished triangles. Given

: <math>X \xrightarrow{s} Y \xrightarrow{s'}Z</math>

with distinguished triangles

: <math>X \xrightarrow{s}Y \to N \to X[+1]</math>

: <math>Y \xrightarrow{s'} Z \to N' \to Y[+1]</math>

where <math>N,N' \in \mathcal{N}</math>, then there are distinguished triangles

: <math>X \to Z \to M \to X[+1]</math>

: <math>N \to M \to N' \to N[+1]</math> where <math>M \in \mathcal{N}</math> since <math>\mathcal{N}</math> is closed under extensions. This new category has the following properties

* It is canonically triangulated where a triangle in <math>\mathcal{T}/\mathcal{N}</math> is distinguished if it is isomorphic to the image of a triangle in <math>\mathcal{T}</math>
* The category <math>\mathcal{T}/\mathcal{N}</math> has the following universal property: any [[exact functor]] <math>F:\mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{T}'</math> where <math>F(N) \cong 0</math> where <math>N \in \mathcal{N}</math>, then it factors uniquely through the quotient functor <math>Q: \mathcal{T} \to \mathcal{T}/\mathcal{N}</math>, so there exists a morphism <math>\tilde{F}: \mathcal{T}/\mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{T}'</math> such that <math>\tilde{F}\circ Q \simeq F</math>.

=== Properties of singularity category ===

* If <math>X</math> is a regular scheme, then every bounded complex of coherent sheaves is perfect. Hence the singularity category is trivial
* Any coherent sheaf <math>\mathcal{F}</math> which has support away from <math>\operatorname{Sing}(X)</math> is perfect. Hence nontrivial coherent sheaves in <math>D_{sg}(X)</math> have support on <math>\operatorname{Sing}(X)</math>.
* In particular, objects in <math>D_{sg}(X)</math> are isomorphic to <math>\mathcal{F}[+k]</math> for some coherent sheaf <math>\mathcal{F}</math>.

=== Landau–Ginzburg models ===
Kontsevich proposed a model for Landau–Ginzburg models which was worked out to the following definition:<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kapustin|first1=Anton|last2=Li|first2=Yi|date=2003-12-03|title=D-Branes in Landau–Ginzburg Models and Algebraic Geometry|arxiv=hep-th/0210296|journal=Journal of High Energy Physics|volume=2003|issue=12|pages=005|doi=10.1088/1126-6708/2003/12/005|bibcode=2003JHEP...12..005K|s2cid=11337046|issn=1029-8479}}</ref> a '''Landau–Ginzburg model''' is a smooth variety <math>X</math> together with a morphism <math>W:X \to \mathbb{A}^1</math> which is [[Flat module|flat]]. There are three associated categories which can be used to analyze the D-branes in a Landau–Ginzburg model using matrix factorizations from commutative algebra.

==== Associated categories ====
With this definition, there are three categories which can be associated to any point <math>w_0 \in \mathbb{A}^1</math>, a <math>\mathbb{Z}/2</math>-[[graded category]] <math>DG_{w_0}(W)</math>, an [[exact category]] <math>\operatorname{Pair}_{w_0}(W)</math>, and a triangulated category <math>DB_{w_0}(W)</math>, each of which has objects

:<math>\overline{P} = (p_1: P_1 \to P_0, p_0: P_0 \to P_1)</math> where <math>p_0\circ p_1,p_1\circ p_0</math> are multiplication by <math>W - w_0</math>.

There is also a shift functor <math>[+1]</math> send <math>\overline{P}</math> to<blockquote><math>\overline{P}[+1] = (-p_0: P_0 \to P_1, -p_1: P_1 \to P_0)</math>.</blockquote>The difference between these categories are their definition of morphisms. The most general of which is <math>DG_{w_0}(W)</math> whose morphisms are the <math>\mathbb{Z}/2</math>-graded complex

:<math>\operatorname{Hom}(\overline{P},\overline{Q}) = \bigoplus_{i,j}\operatorname{Hom}(P_i, Q_j)</math>

where the grading is given by <math>(i-j) \bmod 2</math> and differential acting on degree <math>d</math> homogeneous elements by

:<math>Df = q \circ f - (-1)^df \circ p</math>

In <math>\operatorname{Pair}_{w_0}(W)</math> the morphisms are the degree <math>0</math> morphisms in <math>DG_{w_0}(W)</math>. Finally, <math>DB_{w_0}(W)</math> has the morphisms in <math>\operatorname{Pair}_{w_0}(W)</math> modulo the null-homotopies. Furthermore, <math>DB_{w_0}(W)</math> can be endowed with a triangulated structure through a graded cone-construction in <math>\operatorname{Pair}_{w_0}(W)</math>. Given <math>\overline{f}:\overline{P}\to\overline{Q}</math> there is a mapping code <math>C(f)</math> with maps

:<math>c_1: Q_1\oplus P_0 \to Q_0\oplus P_1</math> where <math>c_1 = \begin{bmatrix} q_0 & f_1 \\  0 &-p_1\end{bmatrix} </math>

and
:<math>c_0: Q_0\oplus P_1 \to Q_1\oplus P_0</math> where <math>{\displaystyle c_{0}={\begin{bmatrix}q_{1}&f_{0}\\0&-p_{0}\end{bmatrix}}} </math>

Then, a diagram <math>\overline{P} \to \overline{Q} \to \overline{R} \to \overline{P}[+1]</math> in <math>DB_{w_0}(W)</math> is a distinguished triangle if it is isomorphic to a cone from <math>\operatorname{Pair}_{w_0}(W)</math>.

==== D-brane category ====
Using the construction of <math>DB_{w_0}(W)</math> we can define the category of D-branes of type B on <math>X</math> with superpotential <math>W</math> as the product category

: <math>DB(W) = \prod_{w \in \mathbb{A}_1}DB_{w_0}(W).</math>

This is related to the singularity category as follows: Given a superpotential <math>W</math> with isolated singularities only at <math>0</math>, denote <math>X_0 = W^{-1}(0)</math>. Then, there is an exact equivalence of categories

: <math>DB_{w_0}(W) \cong D_{sg}(X_0)</math>

given by a functor induced from cokernel functor <math>\operatorname{Cok}</math> sending a pair <math>\overline{P} \mapsto \operatorname{Coker}(p_1)</math>. In particular, since <math>X</math> is regular, [[Bertini's theorem]] shows <math>DB(W)</math> is only a finite product of categories.

=== Computational tools ===

==== Knörrer periodicity ====
There is a Fourier-Mukai transform <math>\Phi_Z</math> on the derived categories of two related varieties giving an equivalence of their singularity categories. This equivalence is called '''Knörrer periodicity'''. This can be constructed as follows: given a flat morphism <math>f:X\to\mathbb{A}^1</math> from a separated regular Noetherian scheme of finite Krull dimension, there is an associated scheme <math>Y = X\times \mathbb{A}^2</math> and morphism <math>g:Y \to \mathbb{A}^1</math> such that <math>g = f + xy</math> where <math>xy</math> are the coordinates of the <math>\mathbb{A}^2</math>-factor. Consider the fibers <math>X_0 = f^{-1}(0)</math>, <math>Y_0 = g^{-1}(0)</math>, and the induced morphism <math>x: Y_0 \to \mathbb{A}^1</math>. And the fiber <math>Z = x^{-1}(0)</math>. Then, there is an injection <math>i:Z \to Y_0</math> and a projection <math>q: Z \to X_0</math> forming an <math>\mathbb{A}^1</math>-bundle. The Fourier-Mukai transform
:<math>\Phi_Z(\cdot) = \mathbf{R}i_*q^*(\cdot)</math>
induces an equivalence of categories
:<math>D_{sg}(X_0) \to D_{sg}(Y_0)</math>
called '''Knörrer periodicity'''. There is another form of this periodicity where <math>xy</math> is replaced by the polynomial <math>x^2 + y^2</math>.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Brown|first1=Michael K.|last2=Dyckerhoff|first2=Tobias|date=2019-09-15|title=Topological K-theory of Equivariant Singularity Categories|eprint=1611.01931|pages=11|class=math.AG}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN356556735_0088?tify={%22pages%22:[159],%22panX%22:0.538,%22panY%22:0.719,%22view%22:%22info%22,%22zoom%22:0.583}|title=Cohen-Macaulay modules on hypersurface singularities I|last=Knörrer|first=Horst|author-link=Horst Knörrer}}</ref> These periodicity theorems are the main computational techniques because it allows for a reduction in the analysis of the singularity categories.

=== Computations ===
If we take the Landau–Ginzburg model <math>(\mathbb{C}^{2k+1}, W)</math> where <math>W = z_0^n + z_1^2 + \cdots + z_{2k}^2 </math>, then the only fiber singular fiber of <math>W</math> is the origin. Then, the D-brane category of the Landau–Ginzburg model is equivalent to the singularity category <math>D_\text{sing}(\operatorname{Spec}(\mathbb{C}[z]/(z^n)))</math>. Over the algebra <math>A = \mathbb{C}[z]/(z^n)</math> there are indecomposable objects

: <math>V_i = \operatorname{Coker}(A \xrightarrow{z^i} A) = A / z^i</math>

whose morphisms can be completely understood. For any pair <math>i,j</math> there are morphisms <math>\alpha_j^i: V_i \to V_j</math> where

* for <math>i \geq j</math> these are the natural projections
* for <math>i < j</math> these are multiplication by <math>z^{j-i}</math>

where every other morphism is a composition and linear combination of these morphisms. There are many other cases which can be explicitly computed, using the table of singularities found in Knörrer's original paper.<ref name=":2" />
